claims.text: A model explicitly incorporating force-constant fluctuations, mass disorder, and anharmonic bonding effects will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than traditional approaches.
FeCoCrMnNi is an example of a compositionally disordered, approximately equimolar high-entropy alloy.
The targeted high-entropy alloys are single-phase, chemically homogeneous solid solutions.
The targeted high-entropy alloys possess significant lattice distortion and chemical disorder.
Effective force-constant fluctuations, Debye temperature, and phonon relaxation times can be calculated from multielement composition and lattice distortion for screening high-entropy alloys.
Mixing multiple principal elements induces lattice distortion and random variations in interatomic force constants.
Lattice distortion and force-constant fluctuations enhance phonon scattering and reduce phonon mean free paths.
Increased configurational entropy produces large variations in atomic masses and local bonding environments.
Mass and bonding-environment variations produce force-constant fluctuations and anharmonicity.
Force-constant fluctuations and anharmonicity lower sound velocities and shorten phonon relaxation times, thereby lowering lattice thermal conductivity.
Alloys with force-constant fluctuations above approximately 20% and lower Debye temperatures should exhibit significantly lower measured lattice thermal conductivity.
Selected high-entropy alloys will have lattice thermal conductivity an order of magnitude below that of comparable homogeneous binary alloys.
Lower intrinsic thermal conductivity improves thermal-insulation performance.
Traditional methods based on averaged bulk properties or simple mixing rules tend to overestimate lattice thermal conductivity because they omit disorder-enhanced phonon scattering.
The predictive approach is expected to be accurate for single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy alloys.
The approach may lose predictive capability when secondary phases, chemical segregation, grain-boundary scattering, or porosity dominate thermal transport.
The exact quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy is not established without calibration against a broad experimental database.
A lack of correlation between predicted disorder descriptors and measured lattice thermal conductivity would falsify the proposed predictive approach.
